title: [Rappler’s Best] A dry spell for ASEAN
summary: ASEAN leaders meet as they grapple with high energy costs, rising food prices, tensions at the border and in the seas, and a feared ‘Super El Niño’ that is seen to reach its peak over the next two…

blocks.text: An all-men ensemble of leaders gathered in Manila on Sunday, November 15, at the start of the 49th ASEAN Summit, representing countries of a region challenged by surging energy costs, rising food prices, tensions at the border and in the seas, and a feared “Super El Niño” that is seen to reach its peak next month. (Check all ASEAN updates, analysis, videos, and photos here.)

Prabowo Subianto, president of Southeast Asia’s largest economy, arrived on Saturday, November 14, from Indonesia — just a few days after his 39-year-old vice president resigned to avoid getting impeached over questionable academic credentials. Political unrest has dampened investor confidence in an economy that has, so far, proved its resilience, which could not be said of Manila, this year’s ASEAN chair.

As President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. opened the summit on Sunday, he did so against the backdrop of the saddest economic numbers that the Philippines has seen in years — GDP growth at 2.1%, making it the region’s economic laggard. He called on fellow ASEAN leaders to “find plans and solutions” to the dire consequences of the Iran war, climate crisis, and regional tensions on millions of households in the region.
Like Prabowo, Marcos has been at war with his vice president, Sara Duterte, who has been impeached by his allies on grounds of unexplained wealth and is now being tried by a Senate impeachment court.

A massive flood control corruption scandal last year, which involved no less than Marcos’ cousin, has turned off investors and stalled government spending on critical infrastructure projects. The Philippines thus has entered “stagflation territory,” as JC Punongbayan put it in this piece.

Ironically, what the Philippines trumpets as a project that will boost livelihood is at the center of protests at the ASEAN Summit: America’s Pax Silica initiative with several countries, including the Philippines. (Police arrested protesters on Sunday, drawing criticism.)

items: Pax Silica, which seeks to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals, and other technologies, is envisioned to be placed in New Clark City, Tarlac.

A leadership shakeup at the agency that runs New Clark City happened last week, with the appointment of Ariel Nepomuceno as new chair of the Bases Conversion Development Authority. Nepomuceno was plucked from the Bureau of Customs, which will now be led by Charlito Mendoza, who was removed from the Bureau of Internal Revenue. Finance Undersecretary Rolando Ligon Jr. has been named acting revenue chief.
The Pax Silica signing between Manila and Washington is eyed before the end of the year.

With US President Donald Trump coming to Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for the ASEAN-US Special Summit, this might be a good opportunity for Marcos to explain what the Philippines wants in the Pax Silica deal, according to JC Punongbayan. Read more.

Marcos could also learn a thing or two on how to deal with Trump from Brazilian President Lula da Silva, who arrived in Manila also on Saturday as a special guest of the President. Read what Lula did here.

blocks.text: What is quite beyond the control of leaders is a very strong El Niño, which the government’s weather bureau predicted to persist until the first quarter of 2027. In Southeast Asia, the United Nations warned that warmer conditions and a lack of rainfall could further damage agriculture.

items: What is the Philippine government doing to prepare? Lourence Angelo Marcellana tells us in this story. Read how farmers are bracing for it.

The following areas may experience drought by the end of November: Albay, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes (Luzon); Capiz, Leyte, Negros Oriental, Samar, Siquijor, Southern Leyte (Visayas); Isabela City, Misamis Oriental (Mindanao). Eirene Manatlao lists down things to expect with Niño. Senators earlier urged Marcos to declare a state of calamity in El Niño-hit areas.

blocks.text: Other highlights from the ASEAN Summit:

items: Business leaders lament the continued failure of ASEAN countries to standardize requirements, investment approvals, and employment requirements — making it difficult for businesses to expand across the region. Read more.

Economic ministers signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which promises smoother cross-border commerce. But as Val Villanueva pointed out in this piece, the real test lies in showing that traders and consumers can capture financial gains.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa said that AI deployment by the private sector has outpaced regulation and control by the government. “Don’t outsource the nuances,” she said. Watch her keynote and fireside chat at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit here.

ASEAN decided to keep the status quo of keeping Myanmar leaders out of its meetings, but opened a “progress-based” path for the country. And as expected, no breakthrough in the years-long efforts to sign the proposed South China Sea Code of Conduct.
